newsitem.title: USA: Pioneer allowed to make broad claims in US patent.
newsitem.headline: Pioneer allowed to make broad claims in US patent.

text.p: Pioneer Hi-Bred International Inc said Thursday that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has allowed the company to make broad claims in its patent application for introducing DNA into corn cells.

Final issuance of the U.S. patent, however, has been suspended while the Patent Office determines if a Pioneer patent would invalidate claims or substantially cover the same invention claimed in any other existing patents or patent applications.

Pioneer said if an overlap between competing claims is found, the U.S. Patent Office likely would declare an "interference." In that proceeding, evidence is presented to prove who created a particular invention first.
Pioneer said it believes it is the first inventor in its claims related to introducing DNA into corn cells.

Several patents have been issued to agricultural companies that produce seeds for crops that are genetically enhanced to withstand the use of certain pesticides or that can fight off certain insects. Several lawsuits claiming patent infringement also have been filed by the companies.
Pioneer said the broad claims allowable in its patent application include the use of particle gun technology as the means to implant DNA into a corn plant.

"We believe this action by the Patent and Trademark Office strengthens the already strong position Pioneer holds in transgenic corn technology, including particle gun-based approaches to the genetic engineering of corn varieties," Charles Johnson, president, said in a statement.

He added that Pioneer is confident that, pending approval by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, it will be able to market advanced corn hybrids that are resistant to the European corn borer in 1997, without paying royalties to another company for the transformation technology.
"In addition, we believe seed companies will likely have to work through Pioneer for freedom to operate with transformation technology in the future," Johnson said.
He said the patent application deals broadly with transformed corn plants, which will help Pioneer's ability in the future to implant other traits genetically, such as resistance to rootworm in corn.
